headline: An ICE agent shot Renee Good. Her family sues the US.
summary: Renee Good's partner and brother announced two lawsuits on Thursday over her death. An ICE officer shot the 37-year-old mother of three in her car at a Minneapolis traffic stop on January 7. One suit says the government's sweep set up "state-sponsored violence". The other names the officer, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem and Tom Homan.
cover_answer: Yes. Renee Good's family just did, twice.
table_question: If someone working for you hurts somebody, is it on you too?

5-7.script: In January an officer in Minneapolis shot a mom named Renee, and she died. Her family thinks the people in charge let it happen, so they are asking a judge to look at it. A judge hears both sides and decides, the way a teacher does when a game goes wrong at recess. You are safe, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Shielded. If it reaches them: one fact, one judge, and your face steady.
5-7.why_long: Shielded: a mother shot in her car is a story a six-year-old can do nothing with, and they read your face before the words. Cantor's work says this age fears harm to a parent above all, so the script moves fast from the shooting to the judge and ends at home. Expect "could that happen to you?" No.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: On January 7 an ICE officer shot Renee Good in her car at a traffic stop in Minneapolis. The government said she tried to hurt agents; her family and witnesses say no. Now her partner and brother are suing the government and the officer's bosses. A lawsuit makes the other side show its work to a judge.
8-12.why: Stop, shot, two accounts, suit. Then show your work.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script hands them the chain in order: stop, shot, two accounts, suit. Showing your work is the mechanism: a lawsuit makes the government lay out what happened before a judge. Expect "did she really try to hurt them?" The government said yes; her family says no.

13-17.script: Who's to blame, the agent or his bosses? Renee Good's family says both: one suit blames the Minneapolis sweep, the other names the officer, Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem and Tom Homan. Second: her mother told Congress she voted for Trump and wants accountability. Does that change how you hear it?
13-17.why: Two suits, two theories of blame.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: an officer pulled the trigger and the people who ran the sweep set the conditions, the way the two suits split it. Her mother's testimony is the second thing, a Trump voter asking for accountability; weighing the source is argument practised. Expect "will they win?" The reports don't say.

5-7.a: An immigration officer did, in January. Her family is asking a judge to say who was wrong. You are safe.

8-12.q: Why sue instead of calling the police?
8-12.a: The shooter works for the government. A suit makes it answer in court.
Hundreds of agents sent to Minneapolis to find immigrants.

13-17.q: Who's to blame, the agent or his bosses?
13-17.a: The family says both: the government, and the officer and his bosses.
Yes. The Federal Tort Claims Act allows it for negligence.
